l: (Joan looks up over her half-moon glasses, a telephone tucked under her chin.) Well, look who's back. Chuck's had me watching the door since seven. (She puts the telephone down.) How was the leave? No, don't tell me. You'll only make me jealous.

You too. Nothing changes: Chuck's upstairs, the coffee's still terrible, and Doris wants you in the Cover Story Department first, through the door on the left. Wherever he's sending you, you're not going as yourself.
(Joan doesn't stop typing.) You know the way: Cover Story's through the door on the left, Chuck's up the stairs, and the coffee's in the cafeteria. I still wouldn't.
(Peggy grins.) Back for more? I'm flying you, wherever it is. We're not going anywhere until Chuck's had his talk with you, upstairs. Then she's all yours.
My name is Chuck. I work at Chuck's Office. I like CIA.
(Doris looks you up and down.) You again. Sit down, let's have a look at you. Hair, clothes, the lot: wherever Chuck's sending you this time, you're not going in a government suit.

There you are. Sit down. Good to have you back. Like the new look. You're going to Sarivalto, an island in the Baltic. Snow, fish, cola and not much else. Its king has just died, and right now nobody knows who's going to run the place.

Everyone. The Communists want the island in the Soviet Union, and Moscow would love a harbour that far north. The royals want the crown kept on Prince Leopold's head. Kelp Cola wants whoever's best for business. The Democrats want a vote. And there's an oil company and a syndicate sniffing around too.

An island that doesn't end up flying a red flag. Your codename is NIGHTJAR. Your cover's a British reporter, from a London paper, there to cover the king's death, so ask all the questions you like. When you're settled in, go and introduce yourself to the island's newspaper, the Eastbrook Gazette: a reporter would. Our man there is Hekki, the radio tech: he's fixed you up a room under his shack, at the radio tower, with a radio set and a screen to reach me on.
You fly out for the first of September, and the island's yours for thirty days. Talk to everyone, help the people who'll help us, and call me every morning. Good luck, NIGHTJAR.
Me again: I'm your ride. It's a long way to the Baltic, and we don't land anywhere anyone can see: a fishing boat meets us off the island at dawn and takes you the rest of the way in. Ready?
(Sam is mending a net on an upturned crate. He nods.) Reporter.
My father's. He knotted it in 1931. I'm mending it. A knot at a time.
(Kaisa slides the headphones off one ear.) Radio Sarivalto, live and slightly out of tune. I'm Kaisa. You're the reporter, the whole island's heard. Don't touch the red button.
Everyone. Communists, monks, oil men. It's the only thing we agree on.
(Hekki looks both ways along the path, twice.) You're NIGHTJAR. You must be. You look exactly like a British reporter, which is the idea, I suppose. I'm Hekki. Radio. And, well. The other thing.
(He drops to a whisper.) Sorry. Sorry. I've been practising. Your room's under my shack: the bookcase, third shelf. Lean on it. It swings.

Radio sets, tape recorders, a bed, a stove, and more tinned soup than one person needs. And the radio set, for calling Chuck: tune it in and call him the minute you're down there. He'll want to hear you've landed. (He swallows.) Welcome to Sarivalto, NIGHTJAR.
"Sorry, I can't think straight. You don't have any food on you, do you?" you ask. Then you've come to the right person. Have a look at what I've got.
(Chuck's voice, thin through the static.) NIGHTJAR, Langley. Good to hear you. Did you make it in one piece?
In one piece. Hekki says hello.

Good. First job: the Communist Party. They want this island in the Soviet Union, and that's exactly what we're here to stop. Their leader is a woman called Anna, at their HQ in Saltwick. Go and talk to her. Friendly. Find out where they stand, and don't tip your hand. Over.
Comrade! Not many come in from the cold to visit us. What brings you to the Party's door?
A journalist! Then write this down: Sarivalto's future lies with the Soviet Union. Moscow will give this island what its kings never did.
NIGHTJAR. You saw Anna? What's the Party really after?
She wants the island in the Soviet Union, and she means it.
That's what I was afraid of. A true believer's harder to deal with than a man with a price. Good work. Get some sleep: tomorrow, Kingsgrad.
(Tiina doesn't look up.) Sirpa's told you everything already, I expect. She'll have told you my name's Tiina. That's all you need to know today.
Is it? You don't know me yet. Wait a week. (The corner of her mouth moves.)
Go on. Sirpa's got more to say than I have.
(Sirpa looks you up and down.) Well! You came in on Tom's boat this morning. Don't look like that: I see everything that comes up this street. Sirpa. And you're the reporter.
Anna's had the Party lights on since five, Lucia came home at three in the morning with sand on her shoes, and Hannu's selling last week's paper again.
(Ray looks you up and down, the way she looks at everyone, and then puts a glass on the bar.) You're the first stranger through that door since the snow came. What'll it be?
Whisky, then. It's the only thing in Saltwick that's been warm since August.
(Hannu snaps his paper shut and beams.) A reporter! Splendid. Colleague, in a manner of speaking. I sell the news. You write it. Between us we're an industry.
'King Dead, Island Mourns.' It was true yesterday and it'll be true tomorrow. A solid story. Keeps its shape.
(Anna is pinning a map of the island to the wall, with Saltwick shaded red.) Only Saltwick's dug out so far, comrade, so only Saltwick matters today. The rest of the island is still under the snow.
Because it's ours: fishermen, gutters, dockers. By the end of the month I'd like a great many more red pins.

Morning, NIGHTJAR. Good work on Anna. The snow's cleared on the road to Kingsgrad, so today it's the palace. The old king's dead, and whoever ends up wearing the crown, or tearing it down, matters to us. Meet the family: Prince Leopold, his brother Augustus and his sister Daphne. And talk to the staff, every one of them. Butlers and maids hear everything.
Good. Be polite, be curious, and remember who said what.

(Hekki watches you squint down the road.) NIGHTJAR, can I say something? You've walked past my tower three times this morning. A spy should know where they are. Hannu sells maps at his newsstand in Saltwick. Three dollars. Will you get one?
Good. Bring it here and I'll mark a few things on it. Small marks. Nothing anyone would notice.
(Hannu shuffles his papers.) Kingsgrad's open. That means a thick Gazette, and a thicker rumour. A man from the palace was seen buying a very large bouquet.
A man told me who told a man. It's all very above board.
(Hekki unfolds it across his knees and takes out a pencil.) Oh, it's the good one. With the contour lines. May I?
(He draws a very small circle.) The Radio Tower. That's us. And a dot by the harbour, where the boats come in at night. If anyone asks, they're places I like the view.

The snow's still blocking the roads north and east. They'll open a bit at a time. Look at the map from your bag whenever you're lost, and you won't walk past my tower again. (He folds it back up, wrongly.)
Kingsgrad's open. (He doesn't look up.) Don't need anything in Kingsgrad.
Once. 1952. Took herring to the kitchens. Cook gave me a bun. Good bun.
(Pat holds up a green glass bottle, corked and waxed.) Look what the sea sent me. There's a letter in it. In Russian, I think: all backwards Rs.
Not yet. You open a thing like that, it stops being a mystery and starts being someone's business. I'm enjoying the mystery.
If you can read Russian, keep it to yourself for now. I like not knowing.
Morning! Oskar, footman. I open the doors, carry the bags and stand very still in the cold. Mostly the cold.
Visitors I've never seen before, coming up the drive late at night. Men in good coats. Mr Edmund says I didn't see them, so I didn't.
Mind the hedges. Viktor. I keep the grounds, such as they are under all this snow.
Do you see much out here?
Everything comes and goes by the front gate, and the front gate goes past my shed. I don't say. Nobody asks a gardener.
A new face! Walk with me, the gardens are the only place in the palace where the walls don't have ears. Well, Viktor has ears, but he only uses them for birdsong.
Who would listen at the walls?
Everyone, darling. The Party, the Americans, the cola people, my own brothers. Half the island wants something from this family, and the other half wants it gone. I find it terribly exciting.
(Oskar stamps his feet on the step.) Sorry. Can't feel my toes. They're in there somewhere, I counted them this morning.
Saving for them. Harbour Outfitters in Saltwick have fur-lined ones, real sheepskin. I'm a third of the way there. The left one, roughly.
You'll want to stand back, this is all starch. Elsa. Every sheet and shirt in the palace comes through this room.
Hard on the hands, easy on the head. And nobody notices a laundress.
Out of my way unless you're carrying onions. Marta. I cook for the family, the staff and every hungry fool who wanders into my kitchen.
What does the prince like to eat?
Herring, like his father. Daphne eats nothing and says it's delicious. Augustus fasts on saints' days, and he's found a lot of saints lately.
Mind the tablecloth, it's just been pressed. Lotta. I set the dining room and clear it again.
They sit together. They don't talk together. It's a long table.
Shh. This is a library. Oh, you're new. Augustus. The other brother. The one who reads.
The lives of the saints. Father Thyme at the monastery lends them to me. They all suffered beautifully. I've not got the knack of it yet.
Good morning. Edmund, butler to the household these thirty-one years. If you've business with the family, you have it through me.
You must know the palace better than anyone.
I know every room, every key and every secret in it, sir. Which is precisely why I keep them.
You'll forgive me if I don't stand. My father's chair is larger than it looks. Are you here to offer condolences, or advice? I've had a great deal of both.

If the island lets me. There are people in Saltwick who'd rather bury the crown with him, and people in Eastbrook who'd sell it. I mean to be crowned. Whether I'm king of anything afterwards is another question.
Oh! I wasn't listening, I was dusting. Ingrid. I keep the royal apartments.
Is it a good place to work?
It's warm and the food's good. You keep your head down and your apron clean.
(Lisa beams from behind the till.) Oh! You're new. You're the reporter, aren't you? From London? Actual London?
I knew it! The coat. Nobody here has a coat like that. Is it true there are shops on every street? Shops on top of shops?
NIGHTJAR. You've been through the whole palace? Tell me what you've got.
Leopold means to be crowned, whatever it takes.
Then he's either our best friend on this island or our biggest headache. We'll find out which. Good work: that's the household on file.
If you hear anything, I'll pay in cigarettes.
(Hekki is polishing a valve.) Chuck came through at dawn, thin but clear. He wants you at the palace. I've written it down, in a code I made up. It's not very good.
Every letter is the one before it. A becomes Z. I thought of it myself.
Hekki, that's the oldest code there is.
Is it? Oh. Well, it's reliable.
(George, faint and crackling.) NIGHTJAR. George. Nothing tonight. When there's a job that needs doing after dark, I'll call. Over.

Morning, NIGHTJAR. Kelp Cola's headquarters in Kingsgrad is open for business. They bottle half the money on this island, and their man Harald wants to lead the Republicans. Go and meet the CEO, Phil. His office is upstairs at the HQ. Find out what kind of man he is.
Good. Drink whatever he pours you.

(Rosa is watching the cola offices, chewing on a pickle.) Phil came in at eight in the blue car. He bought nothing from me. Phil never buys anything from me. Phil eats salad at his desk like a sad rabbit.
Do the cola men talk at lunch?
Constantly. About a new advert, today. A big secret. Phil would faint if he knew I knew. (She taps her nose.) Not a word. Especially not to Phil.

(Harald stands up from his desk, smiling broadly, and shakes your hand with both of his.) The London press! Wonderful! Harald. Kelp Cola. And, if the Republicans will have me, their leader. Sit, sit. You'll want a quote.
(He thinks.) 'What's good for Kelp Cola is good for the island.' No. Too short. Elin will make it longer. Elin makes everything longer, then shorter.
(Elin is typing at a terrific speed and doesn't look up.) Forty calls before the kettle boiled. Phil's upstairs, if it's him you want.
Rosa says you've got a secret.
Rosa says everyone's got a secret. (She types faster.) The annoying thing about Rosa is she's usually right.
Come in, come in! Phil, Kelp Cola. Sit down, have a cold one. On the house. Now, what brings you up to my office?
What do you make of the king's death?

A tragedy. And bad for business: nobody buys when nobody knows who's in charge. This island needs a steady hand, and a steady hand needs a good drink. But you'll never understand us till you've seen where we came from.
We've a museum in Eastbrook. Kelpy gives the tour. Once the snow's off the road, go and take it, then come back here and tell me what you thought. I want to know how it plays to a newcomer.
(Hekki is eating a sandwich over a speaker, very carefully.) The Kelp Cola switchboard is the loudest thing on the island. Forty calls an hour, and every one of them is about money or lunch.
(He thinks about it.) There's no law against it. There's no law for it either. I've decided that means it's encouraged.
NIGHTJAR. You met Phil? What's he like?
Friendly. He wants me to take the tour at his museum.
Then take it, when you can get to Eastbrook. A man who wants you to hear his story wants you on his side. Find out what that's worth to him. Good work. (Kelp Cola: +1 point.)

Morning, NIGHTJAR. The road into Eastbrook's clear. That's Democrat country: timber, coffee and union cards. Their leader's a man called Erik, and he runs things out of the community centre. Go and meet him. Of everyone on this island, they're the likeliest friends we've got. Find out what they need.
Good. Be useful to him. Useful people get told things.
Welcome, welcome! Erik, Democratic Party. Mind the boxes, it's leaflet day. You're the foreign journalist everyone's talking about?

Help? Now there's a word I like. Two of our members could use a friend. Jonna at the tattoo shop hasn't had a customer since the snow came: if you're brave, sit in her chair. And Maya at the Coffee Roasters can't get decent beans since the harbour master started taxing imports. If you know anyone who can bring something in quietly...
I'll see what I can do.
That's the spirit. Either one, or both if you're feeling generous. Eastbrook remembers its friends.
(Jonna is sitting on her own tattoo bench, drawing in a sketchbook.) A customer? An actual person, walking in, upright? I'd forgotten what one looked like. Nobody's been in since the snow came.
(She holds out her arms, inked from wrist to shoulder.) Every one. Some I did myself, left-handed. You can tell which. Don't point them out.
Welcome to Ink and Pine. Something to remember the island by?
(Dex slaps a sausage into a bun and a leaflet into your other hand.) Welcome to the Dogfather! First hot dog in Eastbrook since the snow. Mustard? Ketchup? Democracy? It all comes free with the bun.
Because I make you an offer you can't refuse. One hot dog, one dollar, one leaflet. (He winks.) And because Paolo the bookie told me the Syndicate lot hate it.
Eila and Marjut were on the bench in the cold again, by the west end. (Rosaria wraps two slices in paper.) I take them something every afternoon. Don't tell them I made it on purpose.
Kind? Nobody goes hungry within a hundred metres of my oven. It's a rule. My grandmother's rule. She fed half of Naples in the war.
Hiya, hiya! I'm Kelpy, the Kelp Cola cup! Welcome to the Kelp Cola Museum! The grand tour is five dollars. Ready for the fizz-tory of Kelp Cola?
Follow me! A long, long time ago, before there was any Kelp Cola, there was a beach, and on that beach there was kelp. Lots and lots of kelp! It washed up on the sand after every storm.
Well, our CEO Phil's grandfather gathered up that kelp from the shore, took it home, and brewed it into a health tonic! Folk swore by it: for colds, for aches, for the long winter blues!
Yes indeedy! And over the years the recipe got better and better: a little less seaweed, a lot more fizz! It's been refined and passed down through the family, all the way to Phil.

Ooh, nobody knows! The recipe is a closely guarded secret. Only the family knows it, and it's locked away somewhere very, very safe. Not even Kelpy knows, and I'm made of the stuff! Thanks for taking the tour! The gift shop is right this way!
Come back at lunchtime. By then I'll know everything.
(Hekki holds up a parcel tied with string.) Nothing for you. This is mine: a valve from Helsinki, three months late. I've already named it.
(Hekki looks up from the set.) Phil's sent you to his museum? Go. Pay, smile, buy a postcard. A reporter who takes the tour is a reporter Phil trusts. Keep the receipt. Chuck likes receipts.

Ah! You'll be the reporter from London. Henrik, editor of the Eastbrook Gazette, such as it is: four pages, three staff and a printing press older than me. London sends a reporter to cover our dead king! We're honoured. Come in, come in, meet the team.
Splendid. Nora's over there. She's been dying to meet you. Literally asking everyone in town about you, in fact.
So you're the reporter from London. Funny: I telephoned three London papers this week, and none of them had heard of you. Which paper did you say you were from?
A small one. We cover royal affairs.
A small paper that can afford to fly a man to Sarivalto for a funeral. Must be a very generous small paper.
Hm. Well, welcome to the Gazette, London. If you hear anything about the king's death worth printing, you'll tell me before you tell London. Won't you?
So, our reporter from London! You've met Nora. Don't mind her, she suspects the milkman. Now: what's your story on the king? We'll run it in tomorrow's Gazette too, if it's good.
The empty throne: who will rule Sarivalto?
Now that's a front page! Every faction on the island will buy a copy to see if they're mentioned. Careful, mind: some of them will read it twice.
NIGHTJAR. You met Erik? What did he want?
Help for his members: a tattoo, and some coffee beans.
Ha! Cheapest friendship we'll ever buy. If you need the beans brought in, call me: the diplomatic pouch has room. Good work. (Democratic Party: +1 point.)
The coffee beans for Erik's friend? Sure, the diplomatic pouch has room. Who are they for, exactly?
Maya, at the Coffee Roasters. A Democrat.
Then she gets the good stuff, from Colombia. It'll come in on tonight's drop, and Hekki will have it for you in the morning. Don't make a habit of this.

Morning, NIGHTJAR. The north-east's open, and that means the monastery. Up on the mountain. Don't let the chanting fool you: Father Thyme heads the whole Orthodox Church on this island, and the Church has a lot of say over who sits on the throne. Talk to him, and to every one of his monks. Find out who they'd crown.
Good. Mind the climb, and mind your manners.
Package for you, came in on the night drop. Smells like a coffee shop in Rio. Here you go.
Have you got something for me?
Give Maya the imported coffee beans
Colombian? Real Colombian beans? Oh, you wonderful person. Your coffee's on the house, forever. Well, for a week.

(Maya is writing on a blackboard behind the counter: THIS WEEK'S BLEND: SNOWMELT.) Every week I name a blend. It's the same beans, roasted differently. Mostly it's the same beans, roasted angrily. I'm angrier than usual. Ole the harbourmaster's put the duty on beans up again.
Because the roads are open, and everyone's in a good mood, and nobody's noticed yet that it tastes of bark. Name it something cheerful, they drink it cheerfully.

(Kelpy is waving at a passing tram with both gloves.) Wave at the tram! Everybody waves at the tram! (Whisper.) The drivers wave back. I've counted. Eleven waves this morning. It's the best part of the job.
How long have you been Kelpy?
Six years. Before that, I sang at weddings. Badly paid, well fed. Now I'm well paid and I eat my lunch through a hole in my head.
You took the tour! Well? What did you think?
Best Kelpy we've ever had. Never once taken the head off in public. You'd be amazed how rare that is.

(Wilma is arranging small ceramic Kelpy figurines on a shelf in the gift shop, each exactly an inch apart.) Kelpy figurines. Two dollars. Hand-painted in Kingsgrad. The straw's always the first thing to break. I tell people. They buy them anyway. My husband worked the line here, once.
(She straightens a figurine that doesn't need it.) Arne. He capped bottles from 1951. He's not with us now. Shall I show you the 1951 shelf?
Oh! Forgive me, I didn't hear you come in. Brother Ilja. I copy the old books, and keep the records. Every birth, death and coronation on Sarivalto since the first king.
Always. The line of succession, for one. The late king's grandfather had a brother whom history rather forgot. I've been reading about him. It's probably nothing. It's usually nothing.
Hello. Brother Mikael. You've come up from Kingsgrad? How is it down there? I mean, I don't miss it. I just wondered.
I'd rather not say. Some debts you can pay with money, and some you pay with your whole life. Up here nobody comes looking. Usually.
A guest! Sit, sit, you'll have soup. Brother Teodor. Mushroom, from the forest below. A full stomach is the first step towards a full heart.
It is wonderful. I'd tell you the secret, but then you'd have to take vows. Ha! Eat up.
Another visitor from the towns. Brother Anselm, Prior. You will keep to the paths, you will not photograph the icons, and you will be gone before vespers.
More since the king died than in the ten years before. Party men, oil men, a Russian businessman with expensive shoes. They all want the Abbot's blessing. None of them want his God.
Welcome, child, and catch your breath; the mountain takes it from everyone. I am Father Thyme. Few journalists climb this far for a story. What is it you hope to find?

That is for God, and for the island. But I will say this: a crown is heavier than it looks, and it sits best on a head that has bowed. Prince Augustus comes up the mountain to borrow my books. His brother has never once made the climb.
Mind the cabbages; they're sleeping under the snow. Brother Paavo. I keep the garden, such as it is up here.
Potatoes, cabbages, stubbornness. Things that put their roots down deep and wait out the winter. There's a lesson in that for people, but they never listen. The cabbages do.
(Hekki is wrapping both hands round a mug and shivering.) I've been out on the rocks half the night. If a parcel came for you, it's on the table in your room. I didn't open anything. I smelled one.
Coffee. Very good coffee. (He sighs.) I don't know who you're buttering up, but they're lucky.
NIGHTJAR. You've been up the mountain? What's the Church thinking?
Father Thyme would rather see Augustus crowned than Leopold.
A pious king the Church can steer. Not the worst outcome for us, so long as Moscow doesn't get to Augustus first. Good work. (Orthodox Church: +1 point.)
Good morning, journalist. A friend would like to meet you: the back room of the pizzeria in Kingsgrad. Bring some money of your own, and come alone.
(Chuck's voice, thin through the static.) NIGHTJAR, Langley. Nothing new for you right now. Keep your head down and your eyes open. Over.

(Hekki is staring at the telephone wire that runs into the shack.) Your telephone rang early. I didn't pick it up: it's your line. But I put that line in myself, so I know when it rings. Was it Chuck?
Not really. I can tell you it came through the exchange in Kingsgrad, and the girl on the switchboard was humming. That's all I've got.
(Lisa is looking out of the window towards the harbour.) The delivery boat's late. Third time this month. We're out of milk, eggs and patience.
Where does the boat come from?
Helsinki, every Friday, in theory. In practice, whenever the sea lets it. The captain's called Pekka. He says the sea and he don't get on.
(The back room door is shut, and the sound of chips clicking comes through it.) Busy morning. Some men came early for cards. I gave them coffee and closed the door. Sit, have a slice.
Friends. (She hands you a slice.) The cheese is from Hilda's. Tell me what you think.
(Gustavo does not get up. He gestures at the chair opposite, by the fire.) The journalist. Sit. Nobody at this table will bite you, and the brandy is better than anything in London.
What exactly do you do, sir?
I listen. People come to this table with problems, and they go away without them. It's a kind of public service. Don't put the word 'public' in your paper.
Come back whenever you like. The fire is always lit.
You play like a journalist: carefully, and you watch everyone's hands but your own. Gustavo. I run a few businesses on this island.

Because everyone else will, sooner or later. The Party, the palace, the cola men, the Americans. I like to be first. This island is going to change hands, and when it does, the man holding the cards is the one who knew who was at the table.
Today? You. Write what you like about the island. But if you ever need something brought in, or someone found, you know where the back room is. And Rosaria makes a very good pizza.
NIGHTJAR. I hear you spent the day playing cards. Who with?
Gustavo, the Don. He wanted to meet me before anyone else did.
The Don called you himself? Then he knows more about you than I'd like. Play his game, but don't ever owe him anything. Good work. (Crime Syndicate: +1 point.)
(George, faint and crackling.) NIGHTJAR. George. Nothing tonight. When there's a job that needs doing after dark, I'll call. Over.

(Hekki is bent over a tape recorder, one ear to the speaker.) The Frostholm lines are open, and there's a guest upstairs at the Hotel Aurora who talks to a tape recorder every evening. In Russian. So now I'm taping his tape.
I don't speak Russian. I've got a dictionary, and so far I've translated 'weather', 'cabbage' and 'the Party is pleased'. Chuck will have someone for the rest.

Morning, NIGHTJAR. The north-west's open: Frostholm, the oil rig, the lot. Today it's Diversified Petroleum. Their CEO's an American called Dario: self-made, rich, and he wants everything under the sea round this island. He's one of ours, in a manner of speaking, which is exactly why I don't trust him. Go to their HQ in Frostholm and meet him.
Good. Let him do the talking. He will.

Harald:3.w: Kelp Cola HQ, Kelp Cola HQ

Elin:3.w: Kelp Cola HQ, Kelp Cola HQ
